overview.title: Intersection over Union; compiling and fitting
overview.section: 11.2 Training a segmentation model from scratch
overview.subsection: 11.2.2 Building and training the segmentation model
overview.main_topic: The IoU metric for segmentation, its Keras implementation for the foreground class, and the compile/fit setup with a best-only checkpoint
overview.central_idea: Segmentation quality is measured by IoU = area of overlap / area of union between predicted and true masks. Keras's IoU metric is configured for 3 classes, the foreground class 0, sparse integer targets and dense softmax predictions. The model is compiled with Adam and sparse categorical cross-entropy and trained for 50 epochs, saving the best model.
overview.importance: Pixel accuracy can be misleading when one class (background) dominates; IoU focuses on how well the object of interest is outlined. The sparse/dense flags are a common source of silent bugs.
learning_objectives: Compute IoU from intersection and union of two masks
Configure keras.metrics.IoU for one target class with sparse targets and dense predictions
Explain why sparse_categorical_crossentropy fits integer masks

summary:
The page first completes the sentence from p.339: after compressing inputs to `(25, 25, 256)`, the model *simply applies the corresponding sequence of `Conv2DTranspose` layers followed by a final `Conv2D` layer* to produce outputs of shape `(200, 200, 3)`.

**Intersection over Union (IoU).** To evaluate the model, the authors introduce IoU, a measure of the match between ground-truth and predicted masks. It can be computed separately for each class or averaged over several classes. The recipe has three steps:

1. compute the **intersection**, the area where prediction and ground truth overlap;
2. compute the **union**, the total area covered by both masks, which is *the target object and any extra bits your model might have included by mistake*;
3. divide intersection by union. The result lies between 0 (complete miss) and 1 (perfect match).

**Keras metric.** Rather than coding it by hand, they use `keras.metrics.IoU(num_classes=3, target_class_ids=(0,), name="foreground_iou", sparse_y_true=True, sparse_y_pred=False)`. The callouts explain that `num_classes` is the total number of classes, `target_class_ids=(0,)` selects the class to compute IoU for (0 = foreground), and the targets are sparse integer class IDs *but our model's predictions are a dense softmax!*

**Training.** The model is compiled with `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` (integer masks vs per-pixel softmax) and `metrics=[foreground_iou]`. A `ModelCheckpoint("oxford_segmentation.keras", save_best_only=True)` callback keeps the best model. `model.fit(train_input_imgs, train_targets, epochs=50, callbacks=callbacks, ...)` starts training, and its remaining arguments (`batch_size=64` and the validation data) are on p.341.

paragraphs.excerpt: To evaluate the model, we’ll use a metric named Intersection over Union
paragraphs.what_it_says: IoU measures the match between ground-truth and predicted masks; it can be computed per class or averaged over classes. Step 1: compute the intersection, the area where prediction and ground truth overlap.
paragraphs.what_it_means: For one class c, treat both masks as binary (pixel is c or not) and count overlapping pixels. Averaging per-class IoUs gives 'mean IoU' (mIoU), the standard segmentation benchmark metric (that name is not used in the book).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Background pixels dominate many images; a model predicting 'background everywhere' could have decent pixel accuracy but foreground IoU of 0. IoU exposes this.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Intersection = |P ∩ G| = number of true-positive pixels for class c.

terminology.meaning: |P ∩ G| / |P ∪ G| for predicted region P and ground-truth region G; also called the Jaccard index.

connections: p.337: the foreground class has label 0 after shifting.

paragraphs.excerpt: ground truth overlap. 2 Compute the union of the masks, the total
paragraphs.what_it_says: Step 2: compute the union, the total area covered by both masks, i.e. the target object plus anything the model wrongly included. Step 3: divide intersection by union; the result is between 0 (complete miss) and 1 (perfect match). A built-in Keras metric will be used.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Union = TP + FP + FN pixels. Both false positives (extra bits) and false negatives (missed parts of the object) enlarge the denominator without adding to the numerator, so IoU penalizes both kinds of error.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: IoU cannot be gamed by over-predicting: claiming every pixel as foreground gives full overlap but a huge union.

concepts.name: Intersection over Union (IoU)
concepts.definition: The ratio of the overlap area to the combined area of predicted and ground-truth masks for a class.
concepts.intuition: How much of the 'claimed or true' territory is actually agreed upon.
concepts.technical: IoU_c = |P_c ∩ G_c| / |P_c ∪ G_c| = TP / (TP + FP + FN); in [0, 1]. Keras accumulates TP/FP/FN over batches via a confusion matrix.
concepts.significance: The metric used to evaluate the segmentation model on foreground class 0.
concepts.example: Prediction 1,000 px, truth 900 px, overlap 800 px: union = 1,100, IoU ≈ 0.727.
concepts.misconception: IoU is not pixel accuracy; true negatives (correct background) do not appear in it.

concepts.name: Sparse categorical cross-entropy (per pixel)
concepts.definition: Cross-entropy loss with integer targets, here applied to every pixel's softmax and averaged.
concepts.intuition: At every pixel, penalize the model by how little probability it put on the true class.
concepts.technical: L = −(1/N) Σ_pixels log p_{pixel, y_pixel}, where y is the integer mask label 0–2.
concepts.significance: Lets the uint8 masks from p.337 be used directly without one-hot encoding.
concepts.example: A pixel with true class 0 and predicted [0.9, 0.08, 0.02] contributes −log 0.9 ≈ 0.105.
concepts.misconception: 'Sparse' refers to the label format (integers), not to sparse tensors.

concepts.name: Best-only model checkpointing
concepts.definition: Saving the model only when the monitored validation metric improves.
concepts.intuition: Keep a copy of your best attempt, overwrite it only with better ones.
concepts.technical: keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(path, save_best_only=True), monitoring val_loss by default.
concepts.significance: Recovers the pre-overfitting model reloaded on p.341.
concepts.example: If val_loss bottoms out at epoch 20 and then rises, the file holds epoch 20's weights.
concepts.misconception: It does not stop training; that is EarlyStopping.

math.title: Intersection over Union
math.source_text: 1 Compute the intersection between the masks … 2 Compute the union of the masks … 3 Divide the intersection area by the union area to get the IoU. It's a number between 0 and 1

variables.meaning: Set of pixels predicted as the target class (foreground)
Set of pixels labeled as the target class in the ground truth
Pixels in both P and G
Pixels in P but not G ('extra bits your model might have included by mistake')
Pixels in G but not P (missed parts)

math.operations: Set intersection and union sizes, then a ratio.
math.purpose: Score how well a predicted mask matches the true mask for one class.
math.intuition: Both over- and under-segmentation shrink the score.
math.numerical_example: For a 10 × 10 image, if the true cat covers 30 pixels, the model predicts 35 and they share 25: union = 30 + 35 − 25 = 40 → IoU = 25/40 = 0.625.

math.title: Per-pixel sparse categorical cross-entropy

variables.meaning: Softmax probability vector (3 entries) at pixel (i, j)
Integer label 0, 1 or 2 at that pixel

math.operations: Index the probability of the true class, take −log, average over pixels (and over the batch).
math.purpose: Training objective for the segmentation model.
math.interpretation: Lower is better; 0 when every pixel gets probability 1 on its true class.
math.intuition: Classification loss averaged over 40,000 tiny classification problems per image.
math.numerical_example: Three pixels with true-class probabilities 0.9, 0.6 and 0.3: loss = (0.105 + 0.511 + 1.204)/3 ≈ 0.607.

deeper.title: IoU vs pixel accuracy
deeper.body: Beyond the book: take a 200 × 200 image where the pet covers 10% (4,000 px). A model that predicts background everywhere has pixel accuracy ≈ 90% (ignoring the contour class) but foreground IoU = 0 / 4,000 = 0. A model that predicts the whole image as foreground has foreground IoU = 4,000 / 40,000 = 0.1. Only a model that outlines the pet gets a high IoU.

deeper.title: Why track only the foreground class?
deeper.body: Inference: the task is to separate the main subject from the background (p.335), so class 0 is the one that matters. Background IoU would be high almost for free, and the contour class is a thin ambiguous band with inherently low IoU, so averaging them in would muddy the signal.

It can be computed per class or averaged; here only foreground (class 0) is tracked.

questions.question: A true foreground region has 500 pixels, the predicted one has 600, and they overlap on 400. What is the IoU?
Why is sparse_y_pred set to False?
options: Because the model outputs dense softmax probabilities per class
To compute IoU over all classes
questions.answer: Because the model outputs dense softmax probabilities per class
questions.explanation: Callout: our model's predictions are a dense softmax. Targets are integers (sparse_y_true=True), the flag has nothing to do with sparse tensors, and target_class_ids controls which classes are evaluated.

questions.question: What does target_class_ids=(0,) select and why 0?
questions.answer: IoU is computed only for class 0, which is the foreground (the pet) after the labels were shifted from 1–3 to 0–2.

questions.question: Why does IoU penalize a model that labels every pixel as foreground?
questions.answer: The intersection becomes the whole true region, but the union becomes the whole image, so the ratio equals the fraction of the image that is foreground, typically small.
questions.explanation: The 'extra bits your model might have included by mistake' inflate the union.

questions.question: Which loss is used and why does it fit the data format?
questions.answer: sparse_categorical_crossentropy, because targets are integer class ids per pixel and the outputs are per-pixel softmax distributions.

questions.question: What does ModelCheckpoint(..., save_best_only=True) do here?
options: Stops training when validation loss rises
Saves the model after every epoch
Saves the model only when validation loss improves
questions.answer: Saves the model only when validation loss improves
questions.explanation: save_best_only keeps the best monitored value (val_loss by default). Stopping is EarlyStopping; saving every epoch is save_best_only=False; the whole model is saved, not just optimizer state.
